newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Ecuador/Texaco dispute a "test case".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ecuador/Texaco dispute a "test case".

text.p: The Ecuadoran government's plan to express formal support for the plaintiffs on Friday in an environmental lawsuit against Texaco Inc will be an important test case for such actions, according to lawyers and environmental activists.

"This is the first time that a sovereign state intervenes in a private lawsuit in the United States to protect its citizens," said Henry Dahl, a Texas lawyer representing the Ecuadoran government. "It's a very important precedent."

The case was dismissed earlier this month by a U.S. district court judge who ruled that the U.S. was not the appropriate forum. He cited in his decision the fact that the plaintiffs, indigenous residents of the Amazon rain forest, did not name the Ecuadoran government or state oil company Petroecuador in their suit, though government officials had given conflicting signals about which side they supported in the case.
The plaintiffs and their lawyers hope that the Ecuadoran government's clear support will compel the judge to reconsider.

"It was clearly stated in the judgement that this (intervention) would give the case legs," said Danny Kennedy, coordinator of Project Underground, a non-governmental organization specializing in the mining and oil industries. "Now it's going to fly. We're very excited by this case."

Texaco, which operated in Ecuador from 1964 to 1992, maintains that the case should be resolved in Ecuador. The company says it has nearly completed a program to close abandoned wells and pits and revegetate land.
But the plaintiffs and their supporters say Texaco has not done nearly enough.

"What Texaco did in Ecuador, they would never have done in the U.S.," said Dahl. "If companies understand that they could be held liable in the U.S. for actions abroad, we would live in a safer world."
Punitive damages could amount to "a half billion dollars, but that's something the jury will decide," Dahl said.

When it began extracting oil in Ecuador the early 1970s, Texaco let "process water" from drilling build up in pits and overflow into nearby land and rivers, said Jacob Scherr, a senior lawyer and director of the international program at the Washington, D.C.-based Natural Resources Defense Council.
The council campaigned in 1990 and 1991 for Texaco to set up a $50 million cleanup fund to address the environmental damage in the Amazonian areas where it operated.
"In fairness to Texaco, the standards in the U.S. at the time were also very low when they started off. But the company never upgraded technology as it improved over the years."
The area where the damage was done "is some of the most scarred, depressing and degraded land I've ever seen. There is almost no economic activity underway," Scherr said.

"U.S. courts have been reluctant to get engaged in cases where they could be seen trampling on the sovereignty of other countries. But once that is removed it really becomes a case of the Ecuadoran government operating in concert with the plaintiffs," Sherr said.
Several environmental and human rights goups plan to file amicus briefs in support of the plaintiffs in the Texaco case, according to Kennedy of Project Underground.

However, not all environmentalists were confident that the case against Texaco in the U.S. could be won. "I'm aware of the resources that Texaco has," said Martin Wagner, an attorney with the Sierra Club Legal Defense Fund in Washington D.C.
"The plaintiffs are fighting a really steep uphill battle," he said.
